entries.title: Gloria Steinem, feminist activist and journalist, dies at 92
entries.summary: Steinem became a prominent leader of the second wave of the feminist movement in the US.
entries.content:
United States of America

Gloria Steinem, feminist activist and journalist, dies at 92

September 3, 2026

Steinem became a prominent leader of the second wave of the feminist movement in the US.

Feminist activist and journalist Gloria Steinem has died, her foundation announced Thursday on social media.

She was 92.

Steinem "passed away peacefully at her home in New York City" on Wednesday, her foundation said.

"Gloria's near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end," it added. "Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor."

Who was Gloria Steinem, feminist trailblazer and journalist?

Steinem became one of the most visible symbols of the US women's movement, helping lead the country's second wave of feminism. She was a fierce advocate for feminist causes throughout her life.

She spent the majority of her life on the road, speaking at college campuses, community centers, rallies and marches.

"She spent her recent years doing the two things she loved most: being in community with others and writing," her foundation said.

This is a breaking news story. Please refresh for updates.

entries.title: 'Supersized' El Nino could be strongest on record, UN says
entries.summary: The current El Nino could end up being the strongest since records began 40 years ago, the UN warns. It says the phenomenon is being "supersized" thanks to exceptionally warm temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean.
entries.content:
ClimateGlobal issues

'Supersized' El Nino to persist into 2027, UN says

September 3, 2026

The current El Nino could end up being the strongest since records began 40 years ago, the UN warns. It says the phenomenon is being "supersized" thanks to exceptionally warm temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean.

The El Nino weather phenomenon is set to intensify and will almost certainly last until February next year, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in an update Thursday.

The UN weather agency warned El Nino would develop into a "very strong" event in the coming months, heightening the risks of extreme heat, drought and flooding while threatening livelihoods and economies.

"El Nino is being supersized before our eyes," UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said in a statement. "The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up."

WMO head Celeste Saulo told a press conference in Geneva that, on the current trajectory, the El Nino, "may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began, so literally off the charts we have used for the past four decades."

What is El Nino?

El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that happens every two to seven years and is not caused by climate change. But scientists say it can worsen the impacts of global heating caused by the continued burning of fossil fuels.

The WMO classifies El Nino events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong, with the current El Nino set to reach the highest intensity level on that scale.

The phenomenon begins with the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, triggering changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns around the world.

For example, it often brings dry conditions and drought to Australia, Indonesia and parts of the Amazon, while East Africa and the southern US may experience heavy rainfall.

El Ninos typically begin between March and June, peaking toward the end of the year and lasting around nine to 12 months.

Ocean temperatures already 'exceptionally' high

WMO head Saulo said there was "an exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100% that El Nino will persist through to February 2027," adding that it was the first time the organization had "expressed such a degree of certainty. "

Sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific region , which drive El Nino and reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometers away, are already well above average and continuing to rise, according to the UN agency.

"Subsurface ocean temps are also exceptionally high and in some areas more than 8 degrees Celsius above normal during July and early August," Saulo said.

While El Nino is expected to peak toward the end of the year, its knock-on effects will likely last well into 2027, she added.

Global average temperatures are often particularly high the year after an El Nino. For example, the 2023-2024 El Nino contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record.  

"We should not be surprised if this record is broken," Saulo said.

'We have no time to lose'

Saulo said droughts, floods and extreme heat were already causing disruption and devastation, and warned these impacts would "multiply and cascade as El Nino intensifies."

Saulo stressed that the weather phenomenon would "deliver a major blow to communities, economies and supply chains across the globe" and called for preparations to safeguard climate-sensitive sectors.

"We have no time to lose," she said.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Data centers are everywhere. Here's what they're doing to the planet.
entries.summary: As data centers multiply to meet AI demand, they're straining power grids, draining water supplies, and reshaping the land and air around them.
entries.content:
September 3, 2026

As data centers multiply to meet AI demand, they're straining power grids, draining water supplies, and reshaping the land and air around them.

Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water, and land.

Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia or Sao Paolo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers, is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily.

AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University.  

From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. 

An insatiable appetite for power

Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing sources of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and Internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. 

In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city’s electricity. In Dublin, it’s double that.

And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it’s expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. 

How the AI boom could slow climate progress

All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels.

One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States’ data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. 

The buildout is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone.

And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilos)of coal.

Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. 

However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries.

The hidden water demand

Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation.

A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume.

In Northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region, supply about a third of the world’s online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023.

There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%.

Data centers are making cities hotter

Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside, which can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher tempertures than rural areas.

Researchin Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. 

Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy.

Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing it and piping it into nearby homes and businesses — this process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%.

Coal, gas, and diesel all contribute to dirty air

Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts.

First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities.

On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants.

One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia’s data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. 

The land data centers take over

Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. Repurposing natural and agricultural areas into industrial zones can threaten biodiversity and disrupt local ecosystems.

In Hattersheim, Germany, for example, an 18-acre parcel reserved for agriculture and groundwater protection — a local green space known for its rapeseed blossoms — was rezoned in 2024 to make way for a five-building data center campus.

The damage often extends beyond the site itself. Gas pipelines and power plants built to supply these facilities require their own land, fragmenting habitats and eroding soil along their routes.



Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: India news: Foreign Minister Jaishankar begins Poland, Ukraine visit
entries.summary: Minister S. Jaishankar begins a Poland-Ukraine tour as India steps up diplomatic outreach following Prime Minister Narendra Modi's recent talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India foreign minister begins Poland, Ukraine visit

Published September 3, 2026last updated September 3, 2026

Minister S. Jaishankar begins a Poland-Ukraine tour as India steps up diplomatic outreach following Prime Minister Narendra Modi's recent talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here is a roundup of the latest developments from India on Thursday, September 3.

  • India's foreign minister has begun a three-day tour of Poland and Ukraine
  • US Secretary of State has responded to a key meeting between Indian PM Narendra Modi and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian
  • A retired Air Marshal of the Indian Air Force has been tapped to be the first CEO of the controversy-mired Ram Temple in Ayodhya

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Air Force veteran to be Ram Temple's first CEO

Air Force veteran to be Ram Temple's first CEO

A trust that runs India's grand Ram Temple in Ayodhya has roped in an Indian Air Force veteran to be the Hindu shrine's first chief executive officer (CEO) in a leadership shake-up following a donation embezzlement row, Indian media reported.

Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra, who retired from the Air Force in April 2026, was appointed CEO of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust on Wednesday.

According to news agency ANI, more than 5,000 applicants were vying for the post.

The temple in Uttar Pradesh was inaugurated in 2024 by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, fulfilling a key Hindu nationalist pledge.

The temple site has been a controversial flashpoint because it was built on grounds where the 16th-century Babri Masjid, or Mosque of Babur, once stood. The mosque was demolished by Hindu mobs in 1992, triggering bloody riots that left nearly 2,000 people dead.

Mishra's appointment comes after the Ram Temple became embroiled in controversy in recent months following allegations of theft involving donations and offerings worth millions of rupees.

Mishra served as chief of the Indian Air Force's Western Command during the 2025 Indian military strikes, dubbed Operation Sindoor, which New Delhi said targeted "terrorist infrastructure" in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

"I also consider this the blessings of Lord Ram that after 43 years of service to the nation in the Air Force, He has given me the opportunity to serve Shri Ram Mandir (temple) and Shri Ram bhakt (devotees)," Mishra told news agency ANI.

Opposition slams move

The appointment has also drawn political criticism, particularly in the wake of the donation-related allegations surrounding the temple trust.

The opposition Congress party has questioned Mishra's appointment.

"Will appointing a new CEO or bringing in new people in the Trust bring back the donations by devotees? Has action been taken against the thieves?" Uttar Pradesh Congress chief Ajay Rai said in an interview with ANI.

"Will the retired Air Marshal take action against these thieves and send them to jail? When will the action be taken and the stolen money be brought back?" he added.

Congress leader Imran Masood told news agency PTI that the job was for "saints and seers."

"Now, instead of saints and seers working inside the Ram Temple, a retired Air Marshal will be doing the work," he said.

Skip next section US Secretary of State Rubio reacts to Modi- Pezeshkian meeting

US Secretary of State Rubio reacts to Modi- Pezeshkian meeting

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said he does not believe India and Iran are discussing a trade deal, two days after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modiheld a bilateral meeting with Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the SCO in Bishkek.

The Monday meeting between Modi and Pezeshkian was their first since the start of the Iran war.

Rubio reacted to the leaders' meeting during an interview on "The Brian Kilmeade Show" on Fox News Radio on Wednesday.

When asked by the host whether New Delhi and Tehran were pursuing some form of trade deal, Rubio said: "Well, I don't think there's a trade deal between India and Iran. Obviously, there are - countries all develop their own foreign policy, and many countries around the world talk to the Iranian regime."

Later in the interview, the secretary of state issued a sanctions warning and reiterated US President Donald Trump's stance that no nation should help Iran evade sanctions.

"No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon. And if countries decide to do that, then we're going to have to sanction them too," Rubio said.

Skip next section Foreign Minister S Jaishankar arrives in Poland, next stop Ukraine

Foreign Minister S Jaishankar arrives in Poland, next stop Ukraine

India's External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has reached the Polish capital of Warsaw as he kickstarts an official visit to Poland and Ukraine on Thursday.

During the three-day tour, which runs until Saturday, Jaishankar is scheduled to meet Poland's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha for bilateral consultations, the foreign ministry in New Delhi said in a statement.

The ministry added that the visit is focused on "enhancing bilateral relations" and will also provide an opportunity to "exchange views on regional developments and issues of mutual interest."

The foreign minister was greeted at the airport in Warsaw on Wednesday by India's ambassador to Poland, Neeta Bhushan.

Jaishankar's trip to Poland comes amid speculation about a visit by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to India.

Earlier in August, Poland's top envoy to India said that Tusk's visit, which would be his third to New Delhi, would send a strong signal for cooperation.

There is yet to be formal confirmation of Tusk's India tour.

The visit also reflects broader efforts by New Delhi to deepen engagement with Central and Eastern European partners.

Following the Poland leg of his tour, Jaishankar will head to Ukraine.

Jaishankar's Ukraine visit comes after key Modi-Putin meeting

The Ukraine leg of Jaishankar's tour comes days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Monday. During the meeting, Modi urged an end to the war in Ukraine.

Ahead of Jaishankar's arrival in Kyiv, Ukraine's First Deputy Head of the Office of the President, Sergiy Kyslytsya, said on Tuesday that he had met India's Ambassador to Ukraine, Anjani Kumar, to discuss Kyiv-New Delhi ties and India's role in efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine.

Kyslytsya said he discussed with Kumar Modi's message to Putin in Bishkek, in which the Indian prime minister urged a "move from endless war to end of war" in Ukraine.

"We look forward to continued dialogue with India and to translating this shared interest in peace into concrete steps," Kyslytsya added.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily roundup of the biggest headlines making a splash in India.

India's Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar is embarking on a trip to Poland and Ukraine today, where he is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with his counterparts.

Jaishankar's visit comes on the heels of a meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) earlier this week, where Modi urged close ally Putin to move from an "endless war" to "an end of war" in Ukraine.

In more diplomatic news, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reacted to a meeting between Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.

Meanwhile, in domestic news, Ayodhya's Ram Temple will now have an Air Force veteran as its first chief executive officer following a donation theft controversy.

We will cover that and more in this blog.

entries.title: Germany news: Police say arson attack targeted defense firm
entries.summary: Two people were arrested in connection with a small fire at a construction site in Munich. Police are investigating an attempted attack on a defense company.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Police say arson attack targeted defense firm

Published September 3, 2026last updated September 3, 2026

Two people were arrested in connection with a small fire at a construction site in Munich. Police are investigating an attempted attack on a defense company.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Police in Bavaria are investigating an attempted attack on a defense firm
  • Russia shuts down Germany's 'Goethe Institut' culutral centers
  • Foreign ministers from Germany, France and Poland to meet in Weimar for talks

Read below for a roundup of news and analysis from Germany on Thursday, September 3.

Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google. 

Skip next section German economic institutes raise growth forecasts

German economic institutes raise growth forecasts

Germany's RWI and Ifo economic institutes have lifted growth forecasts for the German economy, citing stronger fiscal spending and exports.

In its latest assessment, the RWI said Germany's economy will grow by 1.3% in 2026, a sharp upward revision from the 0.8% growth predicted in June. The Ifo said German gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to grow by 1.4% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027, both up from previous estimates of 0.8%.

According to the Ifo's assessment, the German federal government's debt-financed investment package and increased demand from abroad are contributing to this positive trend.

The Munich-based institute said that government spending on infrastructure, climate neutrality and defence provided fiscal stimulus worth €40 billion ($46.36 billion), or 0.8% ​of GDP, in 2026.

Both institutes assessed that fiscal spending and exports have been able to outweigh the drag from higher energy prices.

However, RWI cautioned that this export momentum would likely fade later this year because the recent gains were a temporary effect of the rebound from disruptions related to US tariffs last year.

Additionally, the RWI said high ​energy prices, bureaucracy and weak competitiveness continue to weigh on investment.

This comes along with severe weaknesses in Germany's critical automotive industry, which is hemorrhaging jobs and closing factories. 

Skip next section Russia closes Germany's 'Goethe Institut' cultural centers

Russia closes Germany's 'Goethe Institut' cultural centers

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Thursday that Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centers would be closed in Russia.

"Of course they will be closed after our cultural center was expelled from there [from Berlin]," Lavrov said, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.

"They deliberately took this step — they could not have failed to understand — which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia," Lavrov said, according to state news agency TASS.

The comes after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted ‌drone ⁠attack at ⁠the Leipzig/Halle Airport. Germany's response to that incident included closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn.

Goethe operates in around 100 countries worldwide, promoting the study of the German language and providing information about German culture and society.

Russia's first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, shortly after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

The Goethe-Institut is one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia.

Skip next section Police say Munich arson attack may have targeted defense company

Police say Munich arson attack may have targeted defense company

Following an arson attack on a construction site in Munich, the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office (LKA) said Thursday it suspects the fire was an attempted attack on a company involved in the defense industry.

Investigators are looking into a possible political motive, an LKA spokesperson said. The spokesperson did not immediately identify the company involved.

However, the Bild tabloid reported that the fire was set at a construction site near the headquarters of Rohde & Schwarz, a technology company that produces communication systems for the Bundeswehr, among other things.

A spokesperson for the company confirmed the police and fire department response, emphasizing, however, "our company premises themselves are not affected," local public broadcaster BR reported.

Police said multiple incendiary devices were thrown from a vehicle at the construction site in Munich's Berg am Laim neighborhood early Thursday morning around midnight.

According to the LKA, various defense contractors are based in the nearby building complex.

At least one of the incendiary devices sparked a fire that police officers extinguished. Despite the fire, no major damage was caused, a Munich police spokesperson said. However, another incendiary device had to be defused by special forces.

Following a short manhunt, a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man, both Bulgarian citizens, according to BR, were arrested at a nearby gas station, and were being questioned Thursday.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten tag from Bonn.

German media is abuzz this morning about a fire at a construction site in Bavaria that police say was an attempted attack on a defense firm. This comes after two power stations in Germany were the apparent target of sabotage attacks. 

And also today Russia has shut down German cultural centersafter Germany blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack at an airport in August.

entries.title: US, Australia to boost defense ties amid China's growing influence
entries.summary: The two countries said they had agreed to speed up cooperation and boost US military presence in Australia to counter China's unprecedented military buildup.
entries.content:
United States of America

US, Australia to boost defense ties amid China's influence

September 3, 2026

The two countries said they had agreed to speed up cooperation and boost US military presence in Australia to counter China's unprecedented military buildup.

The United States and Australia have announced plans to boost defense ties and strengthen deterrence amid China's growing influence in the Pacific.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met his Australian counterpart, Richard Marles, in Washington on Wednesday, saying Canberra understood "the gravity of maintaining a favorable balance of power in the region."

Marles told reporters that "American force ⁠posture ⁠in Australia is growing" and that the expanding cooperation was a response to "the biggest conventional military build-up by any country in the world since the Second World War in the form of China."

"We need to be ensuring that we build deterrence, that we build balance, so that we can provide for the peace and stability of the region in which we live," he added.

What did the two countries agree?

The Pentagon said the two countries agreed to "accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises."

The force posture initiatives are agreements allowing the US military to train and store equipment in Australia, including the rotational deployment of aircraft and logistics support for US vessels.

While Australia does not permit foreign military bases on its soil, it does host several key joint exercises and rotations of US Marines in the northern city of Darwin. It was not clear if the agreement will see more US troops stationed in Australia.

According to the Pentagon, the two countries also discussed progress on cooperation "to enable shared capacity for guided weapons and next-generation capabilities."

Hegseth said in a statement ⁠that ​there was "strong alignment" between the national defense strategies of both countries.

He also stressed the importance of allies investing in their own sovereign security and the need for them to "both plan together but also ensure our capabilities match and are complementary."

Australia has sought to strengthen its defense force in recent years, focusing on boosting its missile strike capability and deepening strategic alliances.

Cooperation between the US and Australia also includes the AUKUS defense pact with Britain. As part of that pact, American defense personnel are working at the HMAS Stirling naval base in Western Australia, which is set to host a rotating force of US-commanded submarines from 2027.

China has called the AUKUS pact dangerous and warned it could spark a regional arms race.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: US: New York City Mayor Mamdani announces ban on AI for younger students
entries.summary: New York City is barring elementary and middle school students from using generative AI tools this school year. Meanwhile AI literacy classes and supervised pilot programs will be rolled out for high schoolers.
entries.content:
September 3, 2026

New York City is barring elementary and middle school students from using generative AI tools this school year. Meanwhile AI literacy classes and supervised pilot programs will be rolled out for high schoolers.

New York City public schools will temporarily bar elementary and middle school students from using generative artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Wednesday.

Officials have described this as the most expansive such prohibition in the United States.

What do we know about the AI ban?

The one-year moratorium bars student-facing generative AI software for students through eighth grade, affecting roughly 600,000 public school students, while officials study how children use the technology.

The city said the policy will halt use of about 40 educational AI tools currently used in classrooms.. Companion chatbots will be banned across all grade levels.

However, high schoolers will be exempt from the full ban. The city will roll out twice-yearly AI literacy classes for all public high school students and launch pilot programs letting some use select AI platforms under teacher supervision.

Teachers, meanwhile, will still be permitted to use AI for lesson planning and administrative tasks such as scheduling.

What did Mayor Mamdani say about the restrictions?

Mamdani framed the decision around the value of human connection in education: "Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow. They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators and wrestle with tough problems on their own." 

He also tied the policy to the district's broader teaching ideals, saying, "Each day when our children come to school, we teach them to ask questions, to challenge assumptions, to interrogate the premise, to ask why. When it comes to AI in our schools, we hold an obligation to do the same."

New York's move comes as school districts across the country weigh the benefits and risks of generative AI in classrooms.

Is New York alone in banning AI?

New York's move comes as school districts across the country weigh the benefits and risks of generative AI in classrooms.

One of the largest examples is Los Angeles Unified, the US's second-largest school district, which is also temporarily blocking generative AI tools on student devices across all grades as it develops a formal policy this school year. LAUSD had already banned devices before second grade and set screen-time limits as part of a broader policy adopted in June.

Like Los Angeles, New York is pairing AI restrictions with broader limits on technology use.

New York's new plan also includes recommended screen time limits – a cap of 30 minutes daily for grades three to five and 45 minutes for grades six to eight. The plan also calls for a citywide review of education technology tools to eliminate those deemed nonessential to learning.

At least 37 states already have some form of official AI guidance for schools, according to the Associated Press, but no consistent national standard exists for AI literacy instruction.

What has the reaction been?

Reactions from education and advocacy groups were mixed. Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers, welcomed the screen time limits but said the AI policy "leaves many questions unanswered," including how the Education Department will ensure the tools it purchases include adequate safeguards, AP reported.

Josh Golin, executive director of the children's advocacy group Fairplay, told AP he wanted a longer moratorium and more lead time before the school year began, adding that AI platforms should have to "demonstrate that their products are effective at teaching kids, that they're safe, that they're not displacing face-to-face interaction and that they're not leading to rampant cheating."

"A year to evaluate is not nearly enough time," he said.

New York City's roughly 1 million public school students return to classrooms next week.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Russia to close branches of Germany's Goethe-Institut
entries.summary: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the move was in response to Germany's decision to close the Russian House in Berlin after blaming Moscow for an attemped drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia to close branches of Germany's Goethe-Institut

September 3, 2026

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the move was in response to Germany's decision to close the Russian House in Berlin after blaming Moscow for an attemped drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Thursday that Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centers would be closed in Russia.

In remarks carried by Russian news agencies TASS and Interfax, Lavrov said Goethe-Institut branches would be closed in the Russian cities of Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg.

The statement came after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted ‌drone ⁠attack at ⁠the Leipzig/Halle Airport. Germany's response to that incident included closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn.

'End' of German cultural presence in Russia

"Of course they will be closed after our cultural center was expelled from there [from Berlin]," Lavrov said, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.

"They deliberately took this step — they could not have failed to understand — which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia," Lavrov said, according to state news agency TASS.

He added the centers had remained open "despite all the Ukrainian complications in our relations with the West."

What did Germany say?

Berlin said it regretted Russia's decision, calling it unjustified and damaging.

"The Goethe-Institut ... has played an important role in Russia as a cultural bridge, and we would have been prepared to continue that," German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters on Thursday.

He noted that there had "generally always been a good relationship" between the people of Russia and Germany. The "problem," rather, was the Russian leadership, he added.

The foreign minister said Germany and its partners have "always been prepared to engage in a reasonable dialogue with Russia," but stressed that a "prerequisite for this is that Russia finally puts an end to its war of aggression against Ukraine and, above all, refrains from all attacks of any kind against us and our allies."

He said closing branches of the Goethe-Institut as payback for Berlin's closure of the Russian House was unjustified, as the German government's step had been in response to a clear act of aggression by Russia.

Russia has also threatened to take further measures, possibly including the closure of Germany's consulate general in St. Petersburg.

On Wednesday, Russia's Foreign Ministry summoned the charge d'affaires of the German Embassy in Moscow to protest Berlin's response to the August drone incident. According to the ministry, the official was called in over what it described as anti-Russian actions and statements by the German leadership.

On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Moscow for the explosives-laden drone.

What is the Goethe-Institut?

The cultural organization operates in around 100 countries worldwide, promoting the study of the German language and providing information about German culture and society.

Russia's first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, shortly after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

The Goethe-Institut is one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia.

In 2018, Russia ordered the closure of the British Council following a diplomatic dispute with the UK.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: US: 3 dead including suspect in Minneapolis shooting
entries.summary: The motive for the shooting is still unclear. Local authorities and the FBI are responding to the incident.
entries.content:
September 3, 2026

The motive for the shooting is still unclear. Local authorities and the FBI are responding to the incident.

Two people were killed and the suspect also died after a shooting at a downtown Minneapolis apartment building Wednesday afternoon, police said.

Three Minneapolis police officers were injured, Sgt. Garrett Parten said at a news conference Wednesday evening. Two officers suffered gunshot wounds. All three were in stable condition, according to a hospital spokesperson.

One victim was fatally shot at the scene, while the other died after being taken to Hennepin County Medical Center, Parten said.

Minneapolis police responded shortly after 4:30 p.m. local time (21:30 GMT) and urged the public to stay away from the area. Two police officers were among those wounded, officials said. Seven patients were taken to Hennepin Healthcare Medical Center, according to the hospital.

FBI also involved in response as motive unclear

The FBI is responding to the shooting and "will offer any and all resources necessary to assist local authorities," Director Kash Patel said in a post on the social platform X.

No further information was immediately available about the incident. The motive for the shooting is still unclear and information has not been released yet on the identity of the shooter.

Video posted on social media showed police officers aiming rifles toward an apartment tower near the Minneapolis Convention Center. Officials also warned residents to avoid the densely populated Loring Park neighborhood.

"Grateful to law enforcement actively working to ensure the safety of our neighbors in Downtown Minneapolis this afternoon,” Minnesota Governor Tim Walz said. “Minnesota is praying for our first responders.”

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: UNICEF: 1 in 5 youths targeted by online sexual abuse
entries.summary: A survey of around 21,000 young people by the UN's agency for children has found that online sexual abuse of minors is on the rise.
entries.content:
TechnologyGlobal issues

UNICEF: 1 in 5 youths targeted by online sexual abuse

September 3, 2026

A survey of around 21,000 young people by the UN's agency for children has found that online sexual abuse of minors is on the rise.

The internet is not a safe place for unsupervised children and young people — by now, that's common knowledge.

Social media platforms are adept at tweaking their algorithms to ensure users of any age remain on their sites. To do that, they often disseminate content that can be dangerous and upsetting for young people.

Studies regularly find a connection between what's known as doomscrolling and a higher risk of psychological problems in the young, including suicidal thoughts. And some of the latest trends in video creation on platforms like TikTok directly endanger the safety of users.

In the United States, Meta, which owns both Instagram and Facebook, recently opted to settle a case against it out of court. A number of US states had claimed that the two platforms harmed children.

Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion (€14.7 billion) to the states involved and to limit teenagers' access to its platforms to just two hours a day. During the night, access will be completely blocked.

A new survey by UNICEF, the UN agency for children, puts the spotlight on another danger that young people constantly face in the digital world: sexual assault, a threat experienced by one in five people between the ages of 12 and 17 over the past year.

What are the key findings?

The UNICEF report, which DW saw in advance of publication, explains how such attacks often happen.

"It often begins without warning," the authors of the study wrote. "Conversation becomes coercion, and coercion becomes entrapment."

The survey found that more than 15 million children had been exposed to unwanted sexual content. An estimated 9 million were pressured into sexual conversations or asked to share sexual images, while some 4 million had sexual images shared without their consent. The report's authors, however, warn that the true scale is likely far higher.

"The report reveals a painful reality," said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. "These experiences cause profound emotional and mental distress. Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help."

Often, the perpetrator of the assault puts pressure on a victim. The victims then feel ashamed and this makes it difficult to tell anybody about what has happened. Of those surveyed, 41% had never told anybody about their assault. Others said they had first confided in friends, siblings or their mothers. Fewer than 1% were reported to authorities.

The stereotype many have of a complete stranger harassing young people online actually only applies in 16% of cases. Most perpetrators — 57% — are already known to their victims. They may be friends, family members or even romantic partners.

In addition, 27% of respondents were not able to identify the people behind the profiles. When perpetrators are known, they include adults but also minors. In many cases, attacks take place in real life as well as online.

The major social media platforms are also the main gateways for this kind of behavior. The UNICEF report says 60% of assaults come primarily from Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram (all of which are owned by Meta), followed by Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube. And 14% of respondents cited online gaming platforms as the location of an assault — gaming platforms usually have direct messaging channels.

How was the data collected?

The report polled around 21,000 young people in 21 countries, aged between 12 and 17, who regularly use the internet. Data from 12 countries — Ethiopia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Kenya, Malaysia, Mozambique, Namibia, the Philippines, Tanzania, Thailand, Uganda and Vietnam — had already been collected in 2020 and 2021 and analyzed in an earlier report.

For this new report, additional data was collected in Armenia, Brazil, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Pakistan and Serbia. The surveys were also supplemented by longer interviews with 100 young people who had experienced abuse.

Europe, US surveys find similar results

Researchers familiar with this issue would not be surprised by the scale of the problem.

The 2020 EU Kids Online Survey, based on a poll conducted in 19 European countries, indicated that 22% of all participants had received sexually explicit messages online.

In a Spanish study conducted in seven secondary schools in 2021 and 2022, 21% of female respondents said they were sexually harassed online "occasionally," while 5% said this happened "frequently." For male respondents in the Spanish study, the percentages were a few points lower.

A similar survey conducted by the Pew Research Center in 2022 found that 17% of 13- to 17-year-olds in the US said they had been sent explicit images without their consent. The survey did not differentiate between sexually explicit content and other material that showed things like violence.

Social media bans in Australia, UK, France

The UNICEF report calls on governments, tech companies and other stakeholders to better protect children and young people in the digital world.

Among the requests:

  • Design more secure digital platforms, with stronger protection for the privacy of minors.
  • Strengthen national regulations and criminal law, and close loopholes.
  • Establish trustworthy reporting and support systems for young people.

Coming just after Meta's out-of-court settlement in the US, the new UNICEF report will likely add fuel to the fire for those seeking to ban social media for young people, an ongoing debate in many countries.

In December 2025, Australia became the first country in the world to introduce an age limit for social media in order to protect minors. There, anyone under 16 is prohibited from having an account on platforms like YouTube, X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat, a rule the platforms themselves are required to monitor.

A similar age limit will come into effect in the UK in 2027, while France is the first EU country to have passed a law adopting an age limit — 15 years old — for social media users. However, it has since been blocked by France's top court, the Constitutional Council, which ruled it might infringe on freedom of expression and privacy.

In June, a German commission proposed a tiered model. This would come with age limits, requirements for proof of age and strict rules requiring the cooperation of social media platforms.

This article was originally written in German.
